subsystems.name: Telescope and optics
subsystems.role: collects the star's infrared light and keeps the whole observatory cold and stable enough to see a tiny dip.

subsystems.name: Spectrographs
subsystems.role: split the starlight into wavelengths so that absorption by atmospheric gases becomes visible.

subsystems.name: Pointing and sequencing
subsystems.role: holds the star precisely on the detector throughout the transit.

subsystems.name: Data reduction pipeline
subsystems.role: turns raw detector counts into a calibrated transmission spectrum.

subsystems.name: Atmospheric retrieval models
subsystems.role: infers which gases are present and in what amounts.

buildSteps.title: Select a target
buildSteps.detail: Choose a planet known to cross a bright star, with a well-measured orbit from surveys such as Kepler or TESS.

buildSteps.title: Plan the observation
buildSteps.detail: Predict the transit time and duration, then pick the instrument mode and wavelength range that cover the molecules of interest.

buildSteps.title: Observe the transit
buildSteps.detail: Record spectra continuously before, during and after the planet crosses the star, so the star alone can be subtracted.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the raw data
buildSteps.detail: Correct for detector gain, dark current, cosmic-ray hits and drifts in telescope pointing.

buildSteps.title: Extract the light curve
buildSteps.detail: Measure the star's brightness over time in many narrow wavelength bins.

buildSteps.title: Measure the transmission spectrum
buildSteps.detail: For each wavelength, fit the small dip in brightness to get the planet's apparent size at that colour.

buildSteps.title: Fit atmospheric models
buildSteps.detail: Compare the spectrum with synthetic spectra computed from molecular opacities, varying temperature, composition and cloud cover.

buildSteps.title: Validate the result
buildSteps.detail: Repeat with other transits, other instruments or independent pipelines to confirm the signal is real.

prerequisites.why: the atmosphere's absorption features are in the infrared, and the atmosphere itself blocks them from the ground.
you can only study atmospheres of planets whose orbits are known well enough to predict transits.
the signal is a change of a few parts in ten thousand in the star's brightness.
retrieval models need laboratory and theoretical opacities for water, carbon dioxide, methane and other gases.
turning a noisy spectrum into abundances requires radiative transfer and Bayesian inference.
blocking a star's glare to see the planet itself is demonstrated but not yet routine for Earth-sized worlds.

pathway.milestone: JWST characterising gas giants and starting on rocky planets
pathway.unlocks: the first real inventories of exoplanet atmospheres and evidence of clouds and chemistry.

pathway.milestone: dedicated survey missions such as ESA's ARIEL and NASA's Roman Space Telescope
pathway.unlocks: statistical samples of hundreds of atmospheres instead of a handful of case studies.

pathway.milestone: ground-based extremely large telescopes with high-resolution spectrographs
pathway.unlocks: measurements of winds and day-night differences on smaller planets.

pathway.milestone: direct imaging of temperate, Earth-sized planets
pathway.unlocks: the search for gases that could only come from life.
